clinicalPearls: Motor neuronopathy in which weakness and wasting predominate in a scapuloperoneal distribution, affecting shoulder-girdle and peroneal (lower leg) muscles
An autosomal dominant form is caused by variants in TRPV4, a calcium-permeable cation channel, and can overlap with congenital and distal neuropathy phenotypes
Presents with scapular winging, difficulty raising the arms, and foot drop, with a variable age of onset from childhood to adulthood
Sensory involvement is usually minimal, consistent with a predominantly motor neurone or motor axonal process

TRPV4-related disease is notable for its phenotypic breadth, ranging from scapuloperoneal SMA to congenital distal SMA and axonal CMT type 2C, sometimes with vocal cord paresis and skeletal abnormalities
Electrophysiology shows a motor neuronopathy or motor axonal pattern with denervation and preserved sensory responses in the classic forms
Diagnosis requires the characteristic distribution together with genetic confirmation, most often of a TRPV4 variant
reference.pathophysiology: Scapuloperoneal spinal muscular atrophy is a lower motor neurone disorder in which degeneration of anterior horn cells produces weakness in a distinctive scapuloperoneal pattern. The dominant TRPV4-associated form results from variants in a calcium-permeable transient receptor potential channel; the mutations are thought to alter channel gating and calcium handling in motor neurones, leading to selective vulnerability of the neurones supplying shoulder-girdle and peroneal muscles. Because the pathology is largely confined to motor neurones and their axons, sensory function is typically preserved, and the electrophysiology reflects denervation with normal sensory responses. TRPV4 variants can also affect the peripheral nerve and skeleton, explaining the associated phenotypes.
additionalDifferentials: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis in adult presentations
additionalInvestigations: Electromyography and nerve conduction studies showing motor neuronopathy with preserved sensory responses
TRPV4 sequencing and a hereditary neuromuscular gene panel
Creatine kinase and muscle imaging to help separate neurogenic from myopathic causes
Facioscapulohumeral dystrophy genetic testing where the pattern overlaps
Assessment for vocal cord paresis and skeletal abnormalities in suspected TRPV4 disease
Detailed family history for dominant inheritance
redFlags: Vocal cord paresis causing stridor or airway compromise
Rapidly progressive or asymmetric weakness suggesting motor neurone disease
reference.prognosis: Usually slowly progressive with long preservation of function, though severity is variable; congenital TRPV4-related forms and those with vocal cord or respiratory involvement can be more severe.
pitfalls: Confusing the scapuloperoneal weakness pattern with facioscapulohumeral dystrophy
Overlooking the wide TRPV4 phenotypic spectrum, including CMT2C and skeletal features
Assuming a myopathic cause without electrophysiology to identify a neurogenic process
Missing vocal cord involvement that carries airway risk
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists, so manage supportively with physiotherapy to maintain strength and prevent contractures
Provide ankle-foot orthoses for foot drop and occupational therapy and mobility aids to preserve function
Monitor respiratory function and screen for vocal cord paresis, arranging airway intervention if laryngeal involvement causes obstruction
Undertake periodic assessment for the skeletal abnormalities associated with TRPV4-related disease
Coordinate care through a multidisciplinary neuromuscular service
Offer genetic counselling for the autosomal dominant inheritance and testing of at-risk relatives
